notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Land is one of the most important natural resources.
  • It supports:
  • Agriculture.
  • Forests.
  • Settlements.
  • Industries.
  • Transport.
  • Mining.
  • Wildlife habitats.
  • Land is finite in area and cannot be increased substantially.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Land → Finite Resource + Multiple Competing Uses

2. Importance of Land

Land provides:

  • Food production.
  • Housing.
  • Raw materials.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Forest products.
  • Biodiversity habitats.
  • Space for economic activities.
3. Land Use
  • Land use refers to the manner in which land is utilised by people.
  • It reflects both natural conditions and human decisions.

Major uses include:

  • Agriculture.
  • Forests.
  • Pastures.
  • Settlements.
  • Industries.
  • Transport.
  • Mining.
  • Recreation.
4. Factors Determining Land Use

Land use depends on:

Natural factors:

  • Relief.
  • Soil.
  • Climate.
  • Water availability.
  • Natural vegetation.

Human factors:

  • Population.
  • Technology.
  • Economic development.
  • Land ownership.
  • Government policy.
  • Market demand.
5. Land Use Pattern
  • Land-use pattern means the proportion of total land under different categories.
  • It changes over time with population growth, urbanisation and economic development.
6. Reporting Area
  • Land-use statistics are generally compiled for the reporting area for which official land records are available.
  • Reporting area may differ slightly from total geographical area.
7. Major Land-Use Categories in India

Standard land-use classifications commonly include:

  • Forests.
  • Land not available for cultivation.
  • Permanent pastures and grazing lands.
  • Land under miscellaneous tree crops and groves.
  • Culturable wasteland.
  • Fallow land other than current fallow.
  • Current fallow.
  • Net area sown.
📌 Must-Memorise

Land Use → Forest + Non-Agricultural + Pasture + Wasteland + Fallow + Net Sown

8. Forest Land
  • Forest land includes areas officially classified or recorded as forests.
  • Recorded forest land and actual tree cover are not always identical.
  • Forests perform ecological and economic functions.
9. Land Not Available for Cultivation

This broadly includes:

  • Barren and unculturable land.
  • Land put to non-agricultural uses.
10. Barren and Unculturable Land

Examples include:

  • Rocky mountains.
  • Deserts.
  • Steep slopes.
  • Areas unsuitable for cultivation.
11. Land Put to Non-Agricultural Uses

This includes land occupied by:

  • Buildings.
  • Roads.
  • Railways.
  • Industries.
  • Urban settlements.
  • Water bodies in certain statistical classifications.
12. Permanent Pastures
  • Permanent pastures are lands used for grazing livestock.
  • They are important for:
  • Cattle.
  • Sheep.
  • Goats.
  • Other livestock.
13. Grazing Land
  • Grazing land supports livestock feeding.
  • Overgrazing can cause:
  • Vegetation loss.
  • Soil erosion.
  • Land degradation.
14. Miscellaneous Tree Crops and Groves
  • These include lands under tree crops and groves not included in net sown area.
  • Examples can include orchards and groves depending on classification.
15. Culturable Wasteland
  • Culturable wasteland is land capable of cultivation but left uncultivated for a long period.
  • It may require:
  • Reclamation.
  • Irrigation.
  • Soil improvement.
📌 Must-Memorise

Culturable Wasteland → Cultivable but Unused

16. Fallow Land
  • Fallow land is cultivable land temporarily left uncultivated.
  • Leaving land fallow can help restore soil moisture and fertility.
17. Current Fallow
  • Current fallow is land left uncultivated for one agricultural year or a short recent period.
  • It may return to cultivation quickly.
18. Fallow Other Than Current Fallow
  • This refers to land left uncultivated for more than one year but not permanently abandoned.
  • It may be brought back under cultivation.
19. Net Area Sown
  • Net area sown is the actual land cultivated with crops at least once during an agricultural year.
  • If the same field is cultivated twice, it is counted only once in net area sown.
📌 Must-Memorise

Net Sown Area → Physical Area Cultivated at Least Once

20. Gross Cropped Area
  • Gross cropped area is the total area under crops during a year.
  • A field cultivated more than once is counted each time.
📌 Example

One hectare cultivated twice:

Net sown area → 1 hectare.

Gross cropped area → 2 hectares.

21. Area Sown More Than Once
  • Area sown more than once is the difference between gross cropped area and net sown area.
📌 Formula

Area Sown More Than Once

= Gross Cropped Area − Net Sown Area

22. Cropping Intensity

Cropping intensity measures how intensively cultivated land is used.

📌 Formula

Cropping Intensity

= Gross Cropped Area ÷ Net Sown Area × 100

📌 TNPSC Favourite

Cropping Intensity → Gross Cropped Area / Net Sown Area × 100

23. Meaning of 100% Cropping Intensity
  • Cropping intensity of 100% means the net sown area is cultivated only once on average.
24. Cropping Intensity Above 100%
  • A value above 100% means some land is cultivated more than once during the year.
  • Irrigation often increases cropping intensity.
25. Multiple Cropping
  • Multiple cropping means growing more than one crop on the same land within one year.
  • It helps increase production without expanding cultivated area.
26. Factors Increasing Cropping Intensity
  • Irrigation.
  • Short-duration crops.
  • Fertilisers.
  • Mechanisation.
  • Improved seeds.
  • Better market access.
27. Land-Man Ratio
  • Land-man ratio refers broadly to land availability relative to population.
  • As population increases, land available per person generally declines.
28. Population Pressure on Land

High population pressure can cause:

  • Fragmentation of holdings.
  • Intensive farming.
  • Conversion of farmland.
  • Forest encroachment.
  • Land degradation.
29. Land Degradation
  • Land degradation is deterioration in the productive capacity and ecological quality of land.
  • It can result from natural processes and human activities.
📌 Must-Memorise

Land Degradation → Decline in Land Quality/Productivity

30. Major Causes of Land Degradation

Important causes include:

  • Soil erosion.
  • Deforestation.
  • Overgrazing.
  • Mining.
  • Quarrying.
  • Excessive irrigation.
  • Salinity.
  • Waterlogging.
  • Industrial waste.
  • Urbanisation.
  • Unsustainable farming.
31. Soil Erosion
  • Soil erosion removes fertile topsoil.
  • Water and wind are major agents.
  • It reduces agricultural productivity.
32. Deforestation and Land Degradation
  • Removal of vegetation exposes soil.
  • Surface runoff increases.
  • Soil erosion accelerates.
  • Groundwater recharge may decline.
33. Overgrazing
  • Excessive grazing removes vegetation faster than it can regenerate.
  • Bare soil becomes vulnerable to wind and water erosion.
  • Dry regions are particularly vulnerable.
34. Mining

Mining can cause:

  • Removal of vegetation.
  • Soil disturbance.
  • Waste dumps.
  • Water pollution.
  • Land subsidence.
  • Landscape alteration.
35. Quarrying
  • Quarrying removes rock and soil from the land surface.
  • Unregulated quarrying can destabilise slopes and destroy habitats.
36. Excessive Irrigation

Poor irrigation management can cause:

  • Waterlogging.
  • Salinity.
  • Sodicity.
  • Declining soil productivity.
37. Waterlogging
  • Waterlogging occurs when the water table rises close to the surface.
  • Roots receive less oxygen.
  • Agricultural productivity declines.
38. Salinisation
  • Salinisation is accumulation of soluble salts in soil.
  • It is common in:
  • Arid irrigated areas.
  • Poorly drained land.
  • Coastal regions.
39. Urbanisation and Land

Urban expansion converts:

  • Agricultural land.
  • Wetlands.
  • Forest fringes.
  • Open spaces.

into built-up land.

40. Industrialisation and Land Use

Industrial development requires land for:

  • Factories.
  • Warehouses.
  • Roads.
  • Worker settlements.
  • Waste disposal.
41. Infrastructure Expansion

Roads, railways, airports and dams alter land use by:

  • Fragmenting habitats.
  • Converting farmland.
  • Opening new regions to development.
42. Desertification
  • Desertification is land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid regions.
  • It does not mean only the physical spread of an existing desert.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Desertification ≠ Simply Desert Expansion

43. Causes of Desertification
  • Overgrazing.
  • Deforestation.
  • Wind erosion.
  • Poor irrigation.
  • Salinity.
  • Unsustainable cultivation.
  • Drought.
44. Arid and Semi-Arid Vulnerability

Land degradation is serious in parts of:

  • Rajasthan.
  • Gujarat.
  • Haryana.
  • Interior Deccan.
  • Rain-shadow regions.
45. Land Degradation in Rajasthan

Major causes include:

  • Wind erosion.
  • Overgrazing.
  • Vegetation loss.
  • Salinity in irrigated zones.
46. Land Degradation in Irrigated Northwestern India

Important issues include:

  • Waterlogging.
  • Soil salinity.
  • Groundwater decline in heavily pumped zones.
47. Land Degradation in Mineral Regions

Mining-related degradation is significant in parts of:

  • Jharkhand.
  • Odisha.
  • Chhattisgarh.
  • Karnataka.
  • Goa.
  • Rajasthan.
48. Ravine Lands
  • Ravines develop due to severe gully erosion.
  • Chambal basin is India's classic ravine region.
  • Ravines reduce agricultural usefulness.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chambal → Ravines → Gully Erosion

49. Badlands
  • Badlands are severely dissected landscapes with gullies and ravines.
  • They form where erosion has removed much of the fertile soil.
50. Wasteland
  • Wasteland refers broadly to degraded or underutilised land with low productivity.
  • Not all wasteland is permanently useless.
  • Some can be reclaimed.
51. Reclamation of Wasteland

Methods include:

  • Afforestation.
  • Soil conservation.
  • Drainage.
  • Irrigation management.
  • Gypsum application.
  • Rainwater harvesting.
  • Controlled grazing.
52. Reclamation of Saline/Sodic Land

Methods include:

  • Improved drainage.
  • Leaching.
  • Gypsum for sodic soils.
  • Salt-tolerant crops.
53. Reclamation of Ravine Land

Methods include:

  • Check dams.
  • Gully plugging.
  • Afforestation.
  • Grasses.
  • Contour bunding.
54. Reclamation of Mining Land

Measures include:

  • Filling pits.
  • Stabilising waste dumps.
  • Restoring topsoil.
  • Planting vegetation.
  • Treating polluted water.
55. Land Conservation

Land conservation aims to:

  • Maintain soil productivity.
  • Reduce erosion.
  • Prevent desertification.
  • Restore degraded land.
  • Protect ecosystems.
56. Afforestation
  • Afforestation is planting trees on previously non-forested or degraded land.
  • It helps:
  • Stabilise soil.
  • Reduce erosion.
  • Improve water infiltration.
  • Restore habitats.
57. Reforestation
  • Reforestation means restoring tree cover on land where forests were removed or degraded.
58. Afforestation vs Reforestation

Afforestation:

  • Establishing trees on non-forest/degraded land.

Reforestation:

  • Re-establishing forest on previously forested land.
59. Shelterbelts
  • Rows of trees reduce wind velocity.
  • They protect soil from wind erosion.
  • They are especially useful in dry regions.
60. Strip Cropping
  • Crops are grown in alternating strips.
  • This reduces wind and water erosion.
  • It is useful in erosion-prone agricultural areas.
61. Contour Farming
  • Ploughing and planting follow contour lines.
  • This slows runoff.
  • It reduces soil loss on slopes.
62. Terrace Farming
  • Slopes are converted into step-like fields.
  • It reduces runoff velocity.
  • It is common in mountainous regions.
63. Check Dams
  • Small barriers slow runoff.
  • They reduce gully erosion.
  • They trap sediment.
  • They improve groundwater recharge.
64. Watershed Management
  • Watershed management treats land and water as an integrated unit.
  • It aims to:
  • Reduce erosion.
  • Conserve rainfall.
  • Recharge groundwater.
  • Improve vegetation.
65. Farm Ponds
  • Farm ponds store local runoff.
  • They support supplementary irrigation.
  • They also reduce rapid surface runoff.
66. Land Capability
  • Land capability refers to the suitability of land for different uses without causing permanent degradation.
  • Factors include:
  • Soil.
  • Slope.
  • Erosion risk.
  • Drainage.
  • Climate.
67. Land Suitability
  • Land suitability assesses whether a particular land parcel is appropriate for a specific use or crop.
  • It is more use-specific than general land capability.
68. Sustainable Land Management

Sustainable land management aims to balance:

  • Production.
  • Soil conservation.
  • Water conservation.
  • Biodiversity.
  • Long-term productivity.
69. Agricultural Land
  • Agricultural land includes land used for cultivation and related activities.
  • It is influenced by:
  • Soil fertility.
  • Irrigation.
  • Climate.
  • Market access.
70. Net Sown Area Distribution
  • Net sown area is high in intensively cultivated plains.
  • It is relatively low in:
  • Mountains.
  • Deserts.
  • Dense forest regions.
71. Northern Plains Land Use

Major features include:

  • High net sown area.
  • Intensive agriculture.
  • Multiple cropping.
  • Dense settlements.
72. Himalayan Land Use
  • Cultivable land is limited by steep slopes.
  • Terrace farming is common.
  • Forests, grazing and horticulture are important.
73. Peninsular Plateau Land Use

Land use includes:

  • Dry farming.
  • Irrigated agriculture.
  • Forests.
  • Mining.
  • Industries.
  • Plantation crops in suitable areas.
74. Desert Land Use

Important uses include:

  • Pastoralism.
  • Bajra cultivation.
  • Irrigated farming.
  • Solar and wind energy.
  • Mining.
75. Coastal Land Use

Coastal areas support:

  • Agriculture.
  • Fishing.
  • Ports.
  • Industries.
  • Tourism.
  • Aquaculture.
  • Settlements.
76. Wetlands and Land Use
  • Wetlands are often wrongly treated as wastelands.
  • They provide:
  • Flood storage.
  • Groundwater recharge.
  • Fisheries.
  • Biodiversity habitats.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Wetland ≠ Wasteland

77. Conversion of Wetlands

Wetland conversion can cause:

  • Urban flooding.
  • Loss of biodiversity.
  • Reduced groundwater recharge.
  • Water-quality problems.
78. Agricultural Land Conversion

Farmland may be converted for:

  • Housing.
  • Industries.
  • Roads.
  • Commercial development.

This reduces cultivable area.

79. Land Fragmentation
  • Land fragmentation occurs when farms are divided into smaller scattered plots.
  • It often results from inheritance and population pressure.
80. Problems of Fragmented Holdings
  • Difficult mechanisation.
  • Higher boundary losses.
  • Increased travel time.
  • Inefficient irrigation.
81. Consolidation of Holdings
  • Consolidation combines scattered plots into larger compact holdings.
  • It can improve agricultural efficiency.
82. Land Ceiling
  • Land-ceiling laws place limits on the maximum agricultural land that an individual or family can hold.
  • Surplus land may be redistributed according to law.
83. Land Reforms

Land reforms in India have broadly included:

  • Abolition of intermediaries.
  • Tenancy reforms.
  • Land ceilings.
  • Consolidation of holdings.

Detailed economic-policy aspects belong to economy topics.

84. Common Property Resources

Common property resources may include:

  • Village grazing lands.
  • Community forests.
  • Ponds.
  • Tanks.
  • Shared wastelands.

They support rural livelihoods.

85. Commons and Rural Economy

Common lands may provide:

  • Fodder.
  • Fuelwood.
  • Minor forest produce.
  • Water.
  • Grazing space.
86. Encroachment on Common Land

Encroachment reduces:

  • Grazing area.
  • Water-storage space.
  • Biodiversity.
  • Community access.
87. Land Records
  • Land records contain information on:
  • Ownership.
  • Area.
  • Boundaries.
  • Land classification.
  • Cultivation.
  • Accurate records help reduce disputes and improve planning.
88. Cadastral Map
  • A cadastral map shows land parcels, boundaries and ownership-related spatial details.
  • It is used in land administration.
📌 TNPSC Advanced Fact

Cadastral Map → Individual Land Parcels

89. Land Survey
  • Land surveys measure and map land boundaries and physical features.
  • Modern surveys increasingly use:
  • GPS.
  • GIS.
  • Satellite imagery.
90. GIS in Land Management

Geographic Information Systems help:

  • Map land use.
  • Monitor change.
  • Identify degradation.
  • Plan agriculture.
  • Manage forests and cities.
91. Remote Sensing
  • Remote sensing collects information about Earth's surface without direct contact.
  • Satellites are widely used to map:
  • Crops.
  • Forests.
  • Water bodies.
  • Urban areas.
  • Wastelands.
92. Land-Use Change Detection
  • Satellite images from different years can be compared.
  • This reveals:
  • Deforestation.
  • Urban expansion.
  • Crop change.
  • Wetland loss.
93. Urban Sprawl
  • Urban sprawl is uncontrolled outward expansion of built-up areas.
  • It often consumes agricultural and peri-urban land.
94. Peri-Urban Area
  • Peri-urban areas lie at the transition between city and countryside.
  • They often undergo rapid land-use change.
95. Industrial Corridors
  • Industrial corridors stimulate:
  • Factories.
  • Warehousing.
  • Roads.
  • Urban settlements.
  • They can rapidly transform land-use patterns.
96. Mining and Forest Conflict
  • Many mineral-rich regions also contain forests and tribal settlements.
  • Mining can create competition among:
  • Economic development.
  • Forest conservation.
  • Local livelihoods.
97. Shifting Cultivation
  • Shifting cultivation involves temporary cultivation of cleared land followed by movement to another plot.
  • Long fallow periods can allow recovery.
  • Shortened fallow cycles can degrade land.
98. Shifting Cultivation in Northeast India
  • It is commonly known as jhum in northeastern India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Shifting Cultivation in Northeast → Jhum

99. Other Regional Names of Shifting Cultivation

Common traditional names include:

  • Jhum → Northeast India.
  • Podu → Parts of Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Odisha.
  • Kumari → Parts of Western Ghats.
  • Bewar → Parts of central India.
📌 TNPSC Favourite

Shifting Cultivation ↔ Regional Name

100. Dryland Farming
  • Dryland farming is practised in low-rainfall areas without assured irrigation.
  • It depends heavily on moisture conservation.

Important crops include:

  • Millets.
  • Pulses.
  • Oilseeds.
  • Cotton.
101. Rainfed Agriculture
  • Rainfed agriculture depends mainly on rainfall rather than irrigation.
  • Rainfall variability creates production risk.
102. Irrigated Agriculture
  • Irrigation reduces dependence on direct seasonal rainfall.
  • It allows:
  • Multiple cropping.
  • Water-intensive crops.
  • Higher yields.
103. Irrigation and Land Degradation

Poor irrigation can cause:

  • Salinity.
  • Waterlogging.
  • Soil structural deterioration.
104. Command Area
  • Command area is the land that can be irrigated by a canal or irrigation project.
  • Efficient drainage is important in command areas.
105. Cultivable Command Area
  • Cultivable command area refers to the portion of a project's command area suitable for cultivation.
106. Land Levelling
  • Levelling fields helps distribute irrigation water evenly.
  • It reduces runoff and water wastage.
107. Laser Land Levelling
  • Laser technology can create highly level fields.
  • It improves irrigation efficiency and reduces water use.
108. Land and Food Security
  • Agricultural land provides the base for food production.
  • Loss of fertile farmland can increase pressure on remaining cultivated land.
109. Land and Biodiversity
  • Forests, grasslands and wetlands provide habitats.
  • Habitat conversion is one of the major causes of biodiversity loss.
110. Land and Carbon Storage
  • Forests, grasslands and soils store carbon.
  • Land degradation can release stored carbon.
  • Restoration can improve carbon storage.
111. Land and Water Cycle

Healthy land cover:

  • Promotes infiltration.
  • Reduces runoff.
  • Recharges groundwater.
  • Limits soil erosion.
112. Land and Flooding

Conversion of:

  • Wetlands.
  • Floodplains.
  • Agricultural land.

to concrete surfaces increases rapid runoff and flood risk.

113. Floodplains
  • Floodplains naturally store river floodwater.
  • Construction on floodplains increases damage during floods.
114. Coastal Land Use

Coastal land is vulnerable to:

  • Cyclones.
  • Storm surges.
  • Sea-level rise.
  • Erosion.
  • Salinity.

Land-use planning should consider these hazards.

115. Sand Dunes
  • Coastal and desert dunes protect land from wind and waves.
  • Removing dune vegetation destabilises them.
116. Mangrove Land
  • Mangroves protect shorelines.
  • Conversion for settlements or aquaculture may increase coastal vulnerability.
117. Tamil Nadu — Land Resource Overview

Tamil Nadu contains:

  • Agricultural plains.
  • Dry uplands.
  • Western and Eastern Ghats.
  • Forest lands.
  • Coastal plains.
  • River deltas.
  • Urban and industrial land.
118. Tamil Nadu Agricultural Land

Major agricultural landscapes include:

  • Kaveri delta.
  • Western irrigated plains.
  • Southern drylands.
  • River valleys.
  • Tank-irrigated regions.
119. Kaveri Delta Land Use
  • Kaveri delta is dominated by intensive agriculture.
  • Paddy is especially important.
  • Agricultural land depends on:
  • River water.
  • Canals.
  • Northeast monsoon rainfall.
120. Western Tamil Nadu Land Use

Important activities include:

  • Agriculture.
  • Cotton.
  • Turmeric.
  • Horticulture.
  • Industry.
  • Urban expansion around Coimbatore and Tiruppur.
121. Southern Tamil Nadu Drylands
  • Rainfall is relatively low in several interior southern districts.
  • Dryland crops include:
  • Millets.
  • Pulses.
  • Groundnut.
  • Cotton.
122. Nilgiri Land Use

Land uses include:

  • Forests.
  • Tea plantations.
  • Horticulture.
  • Settlements.
  • Tourism.

Steep slopes require careful soil and land management.

123. Eastern Ghats Land Use in Tamil Nadu
  • Hill areas support:
  • Forests.
  • Tribal settlements.
  • Horticulture.
  • Limited agriculture.
  • Soil erosion and deforestation are important concerns.
124. Tamil Nadu Coastal Land Use

Important uses include:

  • Fishing.
  • Agriculture.
  • Salt production.
  • Ports.
  • Industries.
  • Tourism.
  • Aquaculture.
  • Urban development.
125. Salt-Pan Land Use
  • Coastal saline lands in Tamil Nadu are used for salt production.
  • Thoothukudi region is especially important.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Thoothukudi → Salt Production

126. Chennai Urban Expansion
  • Chennai metropolitan growth has converted substantial peri-urban land.
  • Wetland and floodplain protection is important because of intense northeast-monsoon rainfall.
127. Pallikaranai Marsh
  • Pallikaranai Marsh is an important wetland in the Chennai metropolitan region.
  • It performs:
  • Flood-storage.
  • Biodiversity.
  • Hydrological functions.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Pallikaranai → Chennai Wetland

128. Wetlands and Chennai Flood Risk
  • Loss of marshes, lakes and natural drainage channels can increase flood risk.
  • Urban land-use planning must preserve natural water-storage areas.
129. Tank Land in Tamil Nadu
  • Traditional tanks occupy important hydrological space.
  • Encroachment can reduce:
  • Water storage.
  • Groundwater recharge.
  • Flood buffering.
130. Eri Restoration

Restoration of eris can improve:

  • Irrigation.
  • Groundwater.
  • Flood control.
  • Local biodiversity.
131. Land Degradation in Tamil Nadu

Important causes include:

  • Soil erosion.
  • Groundwater overuse.
  • Coastal salinity.
  • Mining and quarrying.
  • Urbanisation.
  • Overgrazing in dry zones.
  • Industrial pollution.
132. Quarrying in Hill Regions
  • Excessive quarrying can:
  • Destabilise slopes.
  • Alter drainage.
  • Remove vegetation.
  • Generate dust.
133. Sand Mining in River Beds

Excessive sand mining can:

  • Deepen river channels.
  • Destabilise banks.
  • Lower groundwater levels.
  • Damage bridges.
  • Harm aquatic habitats.
134. Coastal Sand Mining
  • Removal of coastal sand can accelerate erosion.
  • It can weaken dunes and shoreline protection.
135. Land Restoration

Land restoration means improving degraded land so that ecological and productive functions recover.

Methods include:

  • Afforestation.
  • Soil conservation.
  • Wetland restoration.
  • Mine reclamation.
  • Sustainable farming.
136. Ecological Restoration
  • Ecological restoration aims to recover:
  • Native vegetation.
  • Soil functions.
  • Water cycles.
  • Biodiversity.
137. Land Degradation Neutrality — Concept
  • Land Degradation Neutrality means balancing new land degradation with restoration so that the overall quantity and quality of productive land do not decline.
  • It is an important sustainable-land-management concept.
138. Sustainable Development and Land

Sustainable land use requires:

  • Food production.
  • Urban development.
  • Industry.
  • Forest protection.
  • Water conservation.

to be balanced.

139. Land-Use Planning

Land-use planning identifies the most suitable use for different areas according to:

  • Soil.
  • Slope.
  • Water.
  • Hazards.
  • Ecology.
  • Economic needs.
140. Hazard-Sensitive Land Use

Construction should be carefully regulated in:

  • Floodplains.
  • Landslide-prone hills.
  • Coastal erosion zones.
  • Wetlands.
  • River channels.
141. Land Degradation and Climate Change
  • Degraded soils retain less moisture.
  • Loss of vegetation can increase surface temperature.
  • Land degradation can increase drought and flood vulnerability.
142. Drought and Land

Repeated drought can cause:

  • Vegetation loss.
  • Soil erosion.
  • Reduced organic matter.
  • Desertification.
143. Floods and Land

Floods can:

  • Deposit fertile alluvium.
  • Erode riverbanks.
  • Waterlog fields.
  • Deposit sand over agricultural land.
144. Landslides and Land Resources
  • Landslides remove soil and vegetation from slopes.
  • They can destroy:
  • Roads.
  • Farms.
  • Forests.
  • Settlements.
145. Nilgiris — Land Hazard
  • Nilgiris combine:
  • Steep slopes.
  • High rainfall.
  • Road cutting.
  • Plantation and settlement pressures.
  • These factors increase landslide risk.
146. Land and Renewable Energy

Land is increasingly used for:

  • Solar parks.
  • Wind farms.
  • Hydropower reservoirs.

These projects require careful site selection.

147. Solar Energy Land Use
  • Large solar parks require extensive land.
  • Arid and semi-arid regions often offer high solar potential.
  • Land competition with agriculture and habitats must be managed.
148. Wind Energy Land Use
  • Wind farms are common in high-wind corridors.
  • Tamil Nadu is notable for wind-energy development in southern and western districts.
  • Roads and transmission lines also require land.
149. Tamil Nadu Wind Corridors

Important wind-energy landscapes include areas around:

  • Muppandal.
  • Kayathar.
  • Palghat Gap-influenced western corridors.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Muppandal → Wind Energy

150. Land and Transport

Transport networks consume land but also increase land values and urban growth along corridors.

151. Land-Use Conflict

Common conflicts occur between:

  • Agriculture and urbanisation.
  • Mining and forests.
  • Industry and wetlands.
  • Infrastructure and wildlife habitats.
  • Renewable energy and local land use.
152. Carrying Capacity
  • Carrying capacity is the level of human activity or population that an area can support without severe environmental degradation.
  • It is important in ecologically fragile landscapes.
153. Ecologically Sensitive Areas

Fragile areas include:

  • Western Ghats.
  • Himalayas.
  • Wetlands.
  • Coastal ecosystems.
  • Islands.

Land-use changes here require special caution.

154. Land Use and Western Ghats

Potential pressures include:

  • Quarrying.
  • Roads.
  • Dams.
  • Plantations.
  • Settlements.
  • Tourism.

The region is important for biodiversity and water catchments.

155. Land Use and Eastern Ghats
  • Eastern Ghats face pressures from:
  • Mining.
  • Deforestation.
  • Agriculture.
  • Roads.
  • Settlements.
  • Habitat fragmentation is significant in many areas.
156. Land Use and Islands

Island land resources are limited.

They are vulnerable to:

  • Coastal erosion.
  • Sea-level rise.
  • Tourism pressure.
  • Habitat loss.
157. Land Use and Desert Region

Desert land management focuses on:

  • Dune stabilisation.
  • Controlled grazing.
  • Efficient irrigation.
  • Shelterbelts.
  • Drought-resistant agriculture.
158. Dune Stabilisation

Methods include:

  • Planting grasses and shrubs.
  • Shelterbelts.
  • Restricting excessive grazing.
  • Reducing disturbance.
159. Land-Use Efficiency

Efficient land use means producing more value without unnecessary expansion into forests, wetlands or fertile farmland.

160. Vertical Urban Development
  • Higher-density development can reduce outward urban sprawl when properly planned.
  • However, infrastructure and open-space requirements must also be considered.
161. Brownfield Development
  • Brownfield development reuses previously developed or degraded industrial land.
  • It can reduce pressure to convert new agricultural or natural land.
162. Greenfield Development
  • Greenfield development occurs on previously undeveloped land.
  • It often causes greater land-use conversion.
163. Land-Use Mapping Categories

Satellite-based maps often distinguish:

  • Cropland.
  • Forest.
  • Grassland.
  • Built-up area.
  • Water body.
  • Wasteland.
  • Barren land.
164. TNPSC High-Yield Pairings
  • Net area sown → Cultivated at least once.
  • Gross cropped area → Counts repeated cropping.
  • Cropping intensity → GCA/NAS × 100.
  • Current fallow → Recently uncultivated.
  • Culturable wasteland → Cultivable but unused.
  • Chambal → Ravines.
  • Jhum → Northeast India.
  • Podu → Parts of south/east-central India.
  • Shelterbelt → Wind erosion.
  • Contour farming → Slope erosion.
  • Terrace farming → Mountains.
  • Watershed management → Soil + Water Conservation.
  • Pallikaranai → Chennai wetland.
  • Thoothukudi → Salt pans.
  • Muppandal → Wind energy.
  • Eri → Tamil Nadu tank land.
165. TNPSC Traps
  • Land is a finite resource.
  • Land use and land cover are related but not identical.
  • Net area sown counts a field only once even if cultivated twice.
  • Gross cropped area counts every cropping.
  • Gross cropped area can exceed net sown area.
  • Cropping intensity can exceed 100%.
  • Current fallow is not permanently abandoned land.
  • Culturable wasteland is potentially cultivable.
  • Barren land and culturable wasteland are not the same.
  • Wetlands should not automatically be treated as wastelands.
  • Over-irrigation can degrade land.
  • Desertification does not mean only expansion of the Thar Desert.
  • Chambal ravines result from gully erosion.
  • Mining causes both land and water degradation.
  • Afforestation and reforestation are not exactly the same.
  • Jhum is shifting cultivation of northeastern India.
  • Tamil Nadu's eris are important land-water systems.
  • Urban wetland loss can increase flood risk.
  • Sand mining can lower riverbeds and groundwater levels.
  • Coastal sand removal increases erosion.
  • Sustainable land use requires ecological as well as economic considerations.
166. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Land → Finite.
  • Land use → Human use.
  • Net sown → Once.
  • Gross cropped → Every crop.
  • Cropping intensity → GCA/NAS ×100.
  • Current fallow → Short-term unused.
  • Culturable wasteland → Can cultivate.
  • Degradation → Productivity loss.
  • Chambal → Ravines.
  • Jhum → Northeast.
  • Podu → Shifting cultivation.
  • Contour → Slopes.
  • Terrace → Hills.
  • Shelterbelt → Wind.
  • Watershed → Soil + Water.
  • Wetland → Flood storage.
  • Eri → Tamil Nadu.
  • Pallikaranai → Chennai.
  • Thoothukudi → Salt.
  • Muppandal → Wind.
Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • What is land use? → The way land is utilised for different human and ecological purposes.
  • Major natural factors controlling land use? → Relief, soil, climate and water.
  • Major human factors controlling land use? → Population, technology, economy and policy.
  • What is net area sown? → Physical area cultivated at least once in a year.
  • What is gross cropped area? → Total cropped area counting repeated cultivation.
  • If one hectare is cultivated twice, net sown area is? → 1 hectare.
  • Gross cropped area in the same case? → 2 hectares.
  • Formula for cropping intensity? → Gross Cropped Area ÷ Net Sown Area × 100.
  • Cropping intensity above 100% means? → Some land is cultivated more than once.
  • What is current fallow? → Cultivable land temporarily left uncultivated for a recent agricultural year.
  • What is culturable wasteland? → Land capable of cultivation but left uncultivated for a long time.
  • What is barren land? → Land largely unsuitable for cultivation.
  • What is permanent pasture? → Land used mainly for grazing.
  • What is land degradation? → Decline in land's productive or ecological quality.
  • Major causes of land degradation? → Erosion, deforestation, overgrazing, mining, irrigation problems and urbanisation.
  • What is desertification? → Degradation of land in dry regions.
  • Does desertification mean only desert expansion? → No.
  • What landform is associated with severe gully erosion in India? → Chambal ravines.
  • What is a wasteland? → Degraded or underutilised land with low productivity.
  • Can all wasteland never be used again? → No; some can be reclaimed.
  • How can saline land be reclaimed? → Drainage and leaching.
  • How are sodic soils commonly reclaimed? → Gypsum.
  • How can ravine lands be stabilised? → Check dams, gully plugging and vegetation.
  • What is afforestation? → Establishing trees on degraded or previously non-forested land.
  • What is reforestation? → Restoring tree cover on previously forested land.
  • What do shelterbelts control? → Wind erosion.
  • What does contour farming control? → Runoff and soil erosion on slopes.
  • Terrace farming is suitable for? → Steep hill slopes.
  • What is watershed management? → Integrated conservation of soil and water within a drainage area.
  • What is land fragmentation? → Division of farmland into small scattered plots.
  • What is consolidation of holdings? → Combining scattered agricultural plots into compact holdings.
  • What is a common property resource? → Resource collectively used by a community, such as grazing land or village ponds.
  • What is a cadastral map? → Map showing individual land parcels and boundaries.
  • How is remote sensing useful in land management? → It maps and monitors land-use change.
  • What is urban sprawl? → Uncontrolled outward expansion of built-up areas.
  • What is a peri-urban area? → Transition zone between urban and rural land.
  • Shifting cultivation in Northeast India is called? → Jhum.
  • Podu cultivation is associated with? → Parts of Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Odisha.
  • What is dryland farming? → Farming in low-rainfall areas without assured irrigation.
  • What is rainfed agriculture? → Agriculture dependent mainly on rainfall.
  • What is a command area? → Land that can receive irrigation from a project or canal system.
  • Why are wetlands important land resources? → They store floods, recharge groundwater and support biodiversity.
  • Why is floodplain construction risky? → Floodplains naturally carry and store floodwater.
  • Important Chennai wetland? → Pallikaranai Marsh.
  • Traditional Tamil Nadu tank system? → Eri.
  • Why are eris important? → Irrigation, groundwater recharge and flood moderation.
  • Major salt-producing coastal region in Tamil Nadu? → Thoothukudi.
  • Major Tamil Nadu wind-energy location? → Muppandal.
  • Why is Nilgiri land use sensitive? → Steep slopes, heavy rainfall and landslide risk.
  • Major effect of excessive river-sand mining? → Riverbed lowering, bank instability and reduced groundwater recharge.
  • Why should coastal dunes be protected? → They reduce erosion and protect inland areas.
  • What is land restoration? → Recovery of productivity and ecological function in degraded land.
  • What is sustainable land management? → Use of land while maintaining long-term productivity and ecological health.
